And the Christian philosophers, Quadratus {OCR?} and Aristides, Athenians, composed an apologetic work concerning the doctrine of the Christians.
And Serenus (Serennius?), the governor, also wrote to the emperor
that it is not just to put them to death for the name alone without an accusation.
And the emperor wrote
that they should not die without an accusation.
And in his days the first synod was assembled in Nicaea,
forty-three bishops.
And they anathamatized Sabellius,
who said that there is one hypostasis of the Trinity;
and Valentinus,
who confessed that our Lord brought down a body from heaven.
He who was called Eusebius,
and was surnamed 'the Pious'
and 'Father of the Country',
he and his sons, twenty-two years.
This man commanded that Christians should not be persecuted.
And in his time Galen flourished.
And that he was not in the time of Christ our Lord,
as some people think,
is known from the words of Galen himself.
For he said at the beginning of the first treatise On Anatomical Procedures {OCR?: on dissections}:
"At the beginning, namely, of the reign of Antoninus Caesar,
the first time that I went up to Rome,
I composed the first book On Anatomical Procedures {OCR?: on dissections}."
And he said again in his commentary on the book of Plato's Phaedo:
"We see these people who are called Nazarenes,
who have founded their religion upon signs and wonders,
and are not inferior to those who are truly philosophers.
For they love chastity,
and are constant in fasting,
and are zealous not to commit wrongdoing;
and there are among them people who throughout the whole time of their lives do not approach marriage."
I say
that this is the mark of monasticism,
which was recognized within the space of a hundred years after the ascension of our Lord.
Now there are gathered from the ascension of our Lord until the death of Galen,
according to the exact opinion of the chroniclers,
one hundred and sixty years.
For this Galen was from the city of Pergamon,
and he wrote many books on the craft of medicine;
and they amount—
those of them that are extant—
to about one hundred books.
And it was he who renewed the Hippocratic medicine, which had been neglected.
